name: RPC
model: Call a named operation. This example uses JSON-RPC 2.0.
benefit: A small internal tool can call getOrder with a familiar method name and correlate the reply with request ID 1. The wire format is easy to inspect.
tradeoff: The method name, arguments, and result shape form a contract you must evolve. Retrying a command such as placeOrder after a timeout can repeat its effect unless you design for retries.

name: gRPC
model: Define a typed method in a service contract and call a generated client. Shown here is the method signature.
benefit: Checkout and fulfillment can share a Protobuf contract across languages. The same framework supports streaming for a separate live order-tracking method.
tradeoff: Teams must maintain compatible schemas and generated clients. A browser client typically needs gRPC-Web support at the server or proxy.

name: REST
model: Read an order resource through HTTP’s uniform interface. The server chooses the representation.
benefit: A client can revalidate a previously fetched order with an ETag. The server can return 304 when the representation is unchanged, saving a response body.
tradeoff: A mobile page that also needs shipment details may need another request or a richer representation. Personalized order data needs appropriate cache controls.

name: GraphQL
model: Select fields from a typed schema. The server resolves those fields into the requested shape.
benefit: A phone can request just the status, while a support screen can request the shipment ETA in the same operation. Both use the same schema.
tradeoff: One client request can trigger many backend calls. If a list of orders resolves each shipment separately, batching loads by shipment ID can prevent one extra query per order.
